who: Historian of modern Iran and the Middle East at the University of Pennsylvania; PhD in history, Yale.

evidence.says: The authority identifies the author of Frontier Fictions as a Yale history PhD and, in its 2010 publisher citation, a Penn history professor and Middle East Center director.
Penn's 2013 profile identifies its history professor and Frontier Fictions author, states that she joined Penn in 1999, and describes her Yale graduate studies.
Noor Zehra Zaidi's 2015 Penn history dissertation, Making Spaces Sacred, names Firoozeh Kashani-Sabet as supervisor of dissertation.

notes: The authority's institution, doctorate and book agree with Penn's profile; the listed student's dissertation directly confirms supervision.

who: Historian of Mexico and Latin America at the University of Houston; anthropology PhD, University of Rochester.

evidence.says: The authority links Susan Kellogg, author of Law and the Transformation of Aztec Culture, to Houston's history faculty; its 2024 citation identifies her as Houston professor emerita and an Aztec historian.
Houston's faculty profile describes a historian of Mexico and Latin America who received her anthropology PhD from Rochester.
The department's 2018 PhD list names Susan Kellogg as advisor of both Rikki Bettinger and Daniel Mendiola, with the dissertation titles supplied in the group record.

notes: Direct supervision evidence and the Rochester doctorate establish the match to the Houston historian in the authority.

who: Historian of medieval and early modern South Asia at the University of Chicago; PhD, Jawaharlal Nehru University.

evidence.says: The candidate item describes Muzaffar Alam as a University of Chicago historian, lists Jawaharlal Nehru University among his educational institutions, and carries LC identifier n85107718.
Chicago states that Alam has taught there since 2001, holds a JNU doctorate, and supervises students in medieval and early modern South Asia.
The university repository identifies Muzaffar Alam as an advisor of Elizabeth Lhost's June 2017 PhD dissertation, Between Community and Qanun.

notes: The candidate's institution and field match, with direct repository confirmation for a listed student. Chicago's profile gives inconsistent doctorate years, 1976 and 1977; no year is asserted here.

who: Duke historian of colonial Latin America and the history of sexuality; history PhD, UCLA, 1995.

evidence.says: The authority links Peter Herman Sigal, UCLA history PhD and author of Maya Passions, with the name Pete Sigal on From Moon Goddesses to Virgins.
Peter Sigal's CV records a UCLA history PhD and Duke employment from 2005 onward; its publications use Pete Sigal.
Duke identifies Peter Sigal as professor of history and dates his UCLA PhD to 1995.
The indexed title page of Anderson Hagler's 2022 Duke history dissertation, Curtailing Excess, names Pete Sigal as supervisor.

notes: The authority explicitly bridges Peter Herman and Pete; doctorate, Duke appointment period and a listed dissertation agree.

who: Historian of technology, science and industry in modern East Asia at Harvard; previously Cornell; PhD, Harvard.

evidence.says: The authority identifies Carbon Technocracy author Victor Seow as Harvard history of science faculty since 2017, specializing in technology, industry and the environment in modern East Asia.
Harvard identifies the Carbon Technocracy author, his Harvard PhD in History and East Asian Languages, and his move from Cornell's history faculty to Harvard in 2017.
Cornell's indexed graduate profile names TJ Hinrichs and Victor Seow as Jihyun Han's advisors.

notes: The authority and university profile identify the same scholar. Cornell's explicit co-advisor listing supports the Cornell student entry despite Seow's move to Harvard.

who: William S. McFeely, historian of the Civil War and Reconstruction at the University of Georgia, 1986–1997, then emeritus; Yale American studies PhD, 1966.

evidence.says: The authority connects William McFeely, William S. McFeely and William Shield McFeely; its obituary citation records the Yale American studies PhD in 1966 and Georgia employment from 1986 to retirement in 1997.
Georgia's history department lists William McFeely as professor emeritus.
The department's 2010–2011 newsletter identifies William McFeely as retired in 1997 and working on the Freedmen's Bureau and a biography of Rufus Saxton.

notes: The authority establishes the name variants and Georgia career, overlapping the listed 1992–1996 dissertations. Later completions fall in his emeritus period; individual supervision after retirement was not separately checked.

who: James M. Boyden, historian of early modern Spain at Tulane, formerly Yale; history PhD, University of Texas, 1988.

evidence.says: Tulane records Boyden's Texas history PhD in 1988, Yale appointment in 1988–1991, and Tulane appointments from 1991 onward; he authored The Courtier and the King and has directed or co-directed five PhDs.
The James M. Boyden authority identifies the author of The Courtier and the King as an assistant professor of history at Tulane.
The alternative James W. Boyden authority concerns an attorney credited with The Evidence of the Validity of the Will of Oliver Smith, published in 1847.

notes: James M. Boyden matches the doctorate, field, book and both institutions. James W. Boyden is a different person. The Yale appointment precedes the listed 1995 completions; individual Yale advising was not separately verified.

who: Lorin Lee Cary, labor and social historian at the University of Toledo, 1968–1990; history PhD, University of Wisconsin, 1968.

evidence.says: Toledo's archival biography records Lorin Lee Cary's Wisconsin history PhD in 1968, appointment to Toledo's history department that year, and retirement in January 1990.
The authority identifies No Strength Without Union contributor Lorin Lee Cary as a Toledo professor since 1968 and a 1980 Fulbright-Hays Senior Scholar at the University of New South Wales.
Cary's own biography describes teaching labor and social history at Toledo and co-authoring No Strength Without Union.

notes: The exact doctorate and Toledo career cover all listed dissertation years, 1974–1989; the shared book independently connects the authority to the faculty historian.
